stories.headline: S&P 500 SLIPS FROM RECORD AS RETAIL SALES POST BIGGEST DROP SINCE 2025
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.17% to 7,786 Friday, pulling back from Thursday's record close above 7,800, after July retail sales dropped 0.6% month-over-month -- the sharpest decline since May 2025 and well below the roughly +0.1% consensus. A preliminary University of Michigan reading showed consumer sentiment cooling further in August as households cited both the spending pullback and lingering inflation worries. The index still closed out a third straight weekly gain.
stories.explain: A 0.6% monthly drop in retail sales is a hard growth signal because it's actual spending, not a survey, and motor vehicles (-1.8%) and nonstore/online retail (-2.2%) led the decline while necessities like food services (+0.5%) held up -- a pattern more consistent with consumers pulling back on discretionary and big-ticket purchases than a broad-based recession. That composition matters for the Fed: a narrow, discretionary-led slowdown is easier to look through than a collapse in essentials, which is part of why today's equity reaction was a 0.17% dip rather than a disorderly selloff even after the biggest miss in over a year.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD CLIMBS TO 4.70% AS U.S. SAYS IRAN PORT BLOCKADE COULD RUN 'INDEFINITELY'
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 5 basis points to 4.696% Friday after the U.S. said its naval blockade of Iranian ports could continue indefinitely, even as traders simultaneously digested the weak retail sales print. Oil held its geopolitical premium on the news, with WTI near $82 and Brent near $87-88.
stories.explain: Normally a growth-negative surprise like today's retail sales miss pulls nominal yields down, since it raises the odds of Fed easing and drives flight-to-quality buying. Today it didn't, because the blockade news works through the other half of the yield equation: it raises breakeven inflation expectations by threatening sustained upward pressure on oil, which nominal yields have to price in even as real growth expectations soften. When a supply-side shock and a demand-side shock hit the same day, they pull the same yield in opposite directions -- and today the inflation-risk leg won, which is exactly the kind of stagflationary tension the Fed has to navigate into its September 16 meeting.

stories.headline: BROADCOM SINKS 6% ON $370B AI DEBT-FINANCING QUESTION, DRAGS NASDAQ 100 LOWER
stories.body: Broadcom shares fell roughly 6% Friday after BofA Securities estimated the company's AI chip-financing vehicle could balloon to $370 billion in senior debt by 2029, including about $150 billion of new issuance in 2027 alone. The Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.13% to 30,046 as the selloff rippled through semiconductors, even as AMD gained roughly 4% on a bullish Baird price target.
stories.explain: The $370 billion figure isn't debt sitting on Broadcom's own balance sheet -- it's projected debt in an off-balance-sheet financing vehicle that funds AI chip leases, with Broadcom backstopping some of the customer lease obligations. Markets still punish the stock because a backstop is a contingent liability: if lessees can't pay, Broadcom absorbs the shortfall, so the real economic leverage is larger than the reported balance sheet shows. This is the same structural question hanging over the broader AI capex boom -- how much of the spending is funded by vendor financing and special-purpose vehicles rather than customer cash flow -- and today's move shows investors starting to price that risk into individual names rather than treating AI capex as a uniformly positive catalyst.

stories.headline: GOLD HOLDS NEAR $4,432, UP 1.2% AS WEAKER DOLLAR AND FED-HOLD BETS BUOY BULLION
stories.body: Gold gained about 1.2% to roughly $4,432 an ounce Friday as the dollar index slipped 0.25% to 99.64 and traders raised bets that the Fed will leave rates unchanged at its September meeting rather than hike, building on Thursday's benign core CPI and today's soft retail sales.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so its relative attractiveness moves inversely with real (inflation-adjusted) Treasury yields and with the dollar, since a weaker dollar makes dollar-priced bullion cheaper for foreign buyers. Today both levers moved in gold's favor: falling hike odds cap how far real yields can rise even as nominal yields ticked up on the blockade story, and DXY's slide to 99.64 added a currency tailwind. That combination -- softer growth data lowering the odds of further tightening while a geopolitical premium keeps a safe-haven bid alive -- is the same setup that's driven roughly a month of gold strength.

stories.headline: OIL FIRMS NEAR $82 WTI AS INDEFINITE IRAN PORT BLOCKADE OFFSETS WEAK DEMAND OUTLOOK
stories.body: WTI crude rose about 1.3% to near $82 a barrel and Brent held near $87-88 Friday, as the U.S. Navy's blockade of Iranian ports -- now described as open-ended -- kept a geopolitical floor under prices even after the IEA and OPEC's recent downward revisions to 2026 demand growth.
stories.explain: Oil is being pulled by two forces that don't net out cleanly: a bearish demand signal from IEA/OPEC forecast cuts that traders can act on immediately by selling futures, and a supply-side risk premium tied to the Strait of Hormuz corridor, which carries roughly a fifth of global seaborne crude. An 'indefinite' blockade removes the option of pricing the risk as temporary, so the premium gets embedded further out the futures curve rather than fading -- which is why WTI is up on the day even though the demand backdrop hasn't improved at all.

stories.headline: FIFTH-YEAR ELIGIBILITY RULING RESHAPES PRESEASON TOP 25 AS TRANSFER WINDOW CLOSES
stories.body: A federal judge's ruling granting a fifth season of eligibility to players who began competing in 2022-23 triggered a special Aug. 3-10 transfer window, with Arizona, North Carolina, Tennessee and Gonzaga among the programs adding veteran talent and reshaping early preseason Top 25 projections. Oklahoma landed SMU transfer BJ Edwards (12.7 ppg last season) while Georgetown added DePaul's NJ Benson (11.7 ppg, 7.6 rpg).

stories.headline: NBA UNVEILS 2026-27 SCHEDULE; WESTBROOK RETIRES, CAVS SHIP SCHRODER TO CHARLOTTE
stories.body: The league released its full 2026-27 schedule Thursday, headlined by an Oct. 20 opening-night tripleheader that includes Boston at Detroit; ABC/NBC will broadcast 90 national games, 11 more than last season. Nine-time All-NBA guard and 2017 MVP Russell Westbrook announced his retirement at age 37, and the Cavaliers traded Dennis Schroder and cash to Charlotte for Tre Mann.

stories.headline: PRESEASON WEEK 1 CONTINUES FRIDAY; DOLPHINS DEBUT MALIK WILLIS AT QB
stories.body: Three preseason games kick off Friday at 7 PM ET -- Broncos-Falcons, Dolphins-Commanders and Buccaneers-Jets on NFL Network -- with Miami fans getting their first look at new QB Malik Willis, signed to a three-year, $67.5 million deal after the team moved on from Tua Tagovailoa. Denver's Bo Nix will sit out entirely as Sean Payton manages first-team reps.

stories.headline: FALL CAMPS HEAT UP AS ALABAMA NEARS QB DECISION, OHIO STATE OPENS AS TITLE FAVORITE
stories.body: Alabama is closing in on naming a starting quarterback between redshirt junior Austin Mack and redshirt freshman Keelon Russell, while Washington State plans to name its own starter by Aug. 24. Ohio State enters camp as the betting favorite to win the national title with QB Julian Sayin and WR Jeremiah Smith back under new offensive coordinator Arthur Smith.

sports.detail: Fall camp continues under third-year coach Jedd Fisch, who takes over playcalling duties himself after OC Jimmie Dougherty's February departure. Mock Game and picture day is Aug. 22; season opens vs. Washington State -- Sunday, Sept. 6, 1 PM PT on NBC, Husky Stadium.

After a 16-17 finish (7-13 Big Ten) and no NCAA Tournament bid, UW loses leading scorers Hannes Steinbach (drafted 14th by Charlotte) and Zoom Diallo (transferred to Kentucky). Wesley Yates III (12.9 ppg) returns as Danny Sprinkle rebuilds via the portal in Year 2.

Camp wrapped its 14th session Thursday; CB Terrion Arnold is finalizing a deal with the club, and rookie RB Jadarian Price is drawing praise from teammates. The defending Super Bowl champions open the preseason vs. Dallas -- Saturday, Aug. 15, 5 PM PT, Lumen Field, NFL Network.

Detroit's 2026-27 schedule opens at home vs. Boston on Oct. 20 in the league's opening-night tripleheader (3 PM ET, NBC). The lingering issue: All-NBA Third Team center Jalen Duren remains unsigned more than a month into free agency.
Mariners at Astros tonight in Houston, first pitch 6:10 PM MT / 5:10 PM PT -- game had not yet started as of this brief.

watchlist: FOMC meeting Sept. 16 -- rate-hold odds rising after soft retail sales and Thursday's benign core CPI

deepDive.title: When Weak Data Doesn't Rally Bonds: Growth Shocks vs. Inflation Shocks in Treasury Pricing
content: Today's tape broke the textbook rule of thumb. July retail sales fell 0.6% month-over-month, the worst print since May 2025 and a clean growth-negative surprise -- the kind of number that normally sends Treasury yields lower as traders price in a weaker economy and a more dovish Fed. Instead, the 10-year yield rose about 5 basis points to 4.696%. Understanding why requires splitting a nominal Treasury yield into its two components rather than treating it as a single dial that only responds to growth.

A nominal yield is roughly the sum of a real yield and a breakeven inflation rate, the market's implied forecast for future inflation derived from the spread between nominal Treasuries and inflation-protected TIPS. Weak retail sales should push the real-yield component down, since it signals slower growth and lower future policy rates. But the same day, the U.S. said its naval blockade of Iranian ports could run indefinitely, which raises breakeven inflation by threatening sustained upward pressure on energy prices. When the breakeven leg rises faster than the real-yield leg falls, the net nominal yield goes up even though the growth news was bad.

This is the defining feature of a supply shock versus a demand shock, and it's not a new phenomenon -- it's the same mechanism behind the 1970s oil embargoes and 2022's post-invasion energy spike. In a pure demand-driven slowdown, growth and inflation fall together, so bond yields fall unambiguously and equities and bonds move in the classic inverse relationship investors expect. In a supply-driven episode, growth can weaken while inflation risk stays elevated or rises, so stocks and bonds can sell off or diverge in ways that violate the usual 60/40 portfolio assumptions -- exactly the pattern showing up today with equities down modestly, yields up, and gold up on the same tape.

The practical takeaway heading into the Fed's September 16 meeting is that today's data doesn't cleanly support either a hike or a cut case -- it supports a hold, which is exactly what fed funds futures are now pricing with rising conviction. Watch which leg resolves first: if the blockade eases and oil's risk premium fades, breakevens should fall and pull nominal yields down even if growth stays soft. If the blockade persists while retail spending keeps softening, the Fed faces the classic stagflation bind -- unable to cut without validating inflation risk, unable to hike without deepening the growth slowdown. That tension, not any single data point, is the story to watch into next month's decision.
